MELBOURNE, Oct 12 : New Zealand playmaker Beauden Barrett's confidence suffered during a lengthy spell out of the All Blacks side but the 35-year-old said he harbours no resentment towards coach Dave Rennie. Barrett, capped 146 times by New Zealand, was overlooked for the first six tests of the season before making his return off the bench against South Africa in Baltimore, where he scored a late try. He finally earned a starting berth at fullback against Australia at Eden Park last weekend, helping New Zealand thrash the Wallabies 50-19 to retain the Bledisloe Cup, the annual trophy contested by the trans-Tasman nations, for a 24th straight year. "It did challenge me mentally a little bit," the twice World Rugby Player of the Year said on Monday.

"Not being selected and just feeling a little bit off the pace. When you are in the 23 or the 15 you are in the thick of it, you feel that flow, the connections, the combinations and all of that. "I would be lying if I said that it hasn't affected me, but the important thing is that I have just been able to bounce back and focus on what I do well and be consistent." Barrett, previously first-choice flyhalf under former coach Scott Robertson, found himself down the pecking order after Rennie took charge, with 25-year-old Ruben Love preferred at number 10 and Damian McKenzie at fullback. He was relegated to helping the match-day squad prepare at training, but said he had worked hard to regain his confidence. Injuries to Love and Richie Mo'unga have since opened the door for Barrett, who hopes to retain his place for Saturday's second Bledisloe Cup test in Sydney. Barrett said Rennie had been forthright about his standing in the squad. "He was telling me he was liking how I was training, he was happy with my contribution and it was clear that I wasn't up in the pecking order, so I had to really work for it or wait for my opportunity," he added. "We are both honest with one another, we know where we stand and there are no mixed messages."

Source: Reuters

NEW DELHI: Authorities closed six metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions in Delhi on Monday (Oct 12), as opposition parties planned to march to the Supreme Court in protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has sparked days of unrest in the Indian capital. Opposition parties and supporters of the "cockroach" youth movemen t have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the revision that critics say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).  The revision that started last year saw over 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists , including the dead, the relocated and people who could not be traced.     Police detained thousands of protesters in Delhi over the weekend, including leaders of the "Cockroach Janta Party" (CJP) , as supporters of the youth movement sought to march in protest and were stopped by thousands of security personnel who locked down central Delhi.

The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine the country's democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.  Six metro stations were closed on Monday for "security reasons", and police imposed traffic restrictions and diversions along over 20 stretches.   The main opposition Congress party announced a march to the Supreme Court to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice demanding an end to what it calls "vote theft" and Kumar's resignation. "Youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the Constitution of India, will walk with us," Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on X.

India's Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel stand guard, amid protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi on Oct 11, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Bhawika Chhabra)

COCKROACH MOVEMENT TO SEEK PERMISSION FOR NEW PROTEST Chief Justice Surya Kant, however, declined the meeting request in an email, saying Gandhi and the Congress delegation should instead approach the court legally since the issue is already being heard by the court and should be addressed through judicial proceedings, a Congress source said. Separately, the CJP said its leaders would meet Delhi Police to "demand" a date for a peaceful protest. It has threatened to announce a new protest call if a date is not given within 24 hours.  The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months against issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs, is one of the biggest political challenges to Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power. The protests erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported last month that Kumar's two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems. Election Commission data shows about 130 million names have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 28 million people who had died, 63 million who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced. Opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions – charges both the poll panel and BJP reject.

NEW DELHI, Oct 12 : Oil prices slipped on Monday on expectations of more Russian supplies after US President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy facilities following a US diesel-supply deal with Moscow. Brent crude futures fell 11 cents, or 0.11 per cent, to $104.61 a barrel by 0627 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $91.36 a barrel, down 49 cents, or 0.53 per cent. Both benchmarks were down more than 1 per cent earlier in the session. ICE gasoil futures fell 3 per cent to $1,436 per metric ton after President Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons "immediately thereafter", Trump added. The daily diesel consumption globally is forecast at close to 29 million barrels, according to the International Energy Agency.

Trump also unexpectedly announced on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details of the energy ceasefire while Russia did not comment. The announcements eased some of the immediate supply pressure, Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said. "Questions remain over the validity and longevity of any such ceasefire, and without clearer evidence that it will actually hold, the extent of the pullback is likely to stay limited," he added. IEA's Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Sunday that all members should assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and that countries which have not yet fully delivered pledged volumes accelerate their remaining releases prioritising diesel. CRUDE SUPPORTED BY MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT However, the Middle East conflict continued to support Brent crude at above $100 a barrel. The Houthis claimed responsibility for a Saturday strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while Saudi authorities reported that people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. In addition, more attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz have been reported so far this month, threatening to dampen a recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September. A tanker was struck by a drone in the vicinity of Sohar anchorage, Oman, while another was damaged by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported over the weekend. Goldman Sachs raised its Brent crude price forecast for December to $90 a barrel, up from $85 previously, its analysts led by Daan Struyven said in a note. "We maintain our base case that continued adaptation of Mideast supply will eventually reduce crude oil prices, while potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk," the analysts said, estimating a risk premium of just over $20 a barrel. "We forecast WTI prices, which are unusually low vs Brent because of high US-Europe shipping costs, to average $81 in December 2026 and $73 in 2027," they added. In the Gulf of Mexico, energy majors Shell, Chevron and BP were seeking to redeploy personnel and restore production at their platforms after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday.

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK: Pakistan's economy is expected to grow by more than 4 per cent this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices, as the government looks to push for the privatisation of five to six entities that could raise upwards of US$1 billion, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters on Monday (Oct 12). Pakistan's economy is considered to be highly vulnerable to a prolonged Middle East conflict given its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region, even as it remains reliant on external financing to bolster foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments. The South Asian country of 255 million people has been able to procure adequate quantities of fuel, successfully avoiding any shortages, and critical sectors such as agriculture were holding up, Aurangzeb said. "So I'm still quite clear that we should clock north of 4 per cent," he said in an interview on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.

"And on the inflation side, obviously, we are keeping a very close eye because it does have a knock-on impact in terms of the commodity prices." Following a period of severe economic turmoil exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, the cash-strapped economy has recovered some of its footing, supported by a US$7 billion, 37-month IMF loan program known as the Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 that includes some tough measures such as raising tax revenue on farm income. EXCHANGE STABILISATION FACILITY  The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the meetings that are being held outside Washington for the first time in three years. Pakistan, which reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF last week potentially unlocking about US$1.21 billion in financing under the Extended Fund Facility and a climate program, is continuing discussions with the United States for a proposed US$10 billion exchange stabilisation facility, Aurangzeb said. But he declined to provide a time frame for the conclusion of negotiations. "If it comes through, this will be a great help for us," he said, referring to the facility, which is in addition to ongoing talks with the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) and the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC). "If it doesn't come through, this does not, you know, create any problem for us in terms of access to market." PRIVATISATION PUSH Following the privatisation of flag carrier Pakistan International Airlines last year, Aurangzeb said the government has around another dozen entities in the pipeline, including state-owned power distribution companies and the outsourcing of airport operations. "I expect about five or six of these to go through during this fiscal year," he said, adding that they could raise more than US$1 billion. Privatisation has been seen as a key test of Pakistan's reform credibility with the IMF, with officials previously underlining that failure to offload loss-making state firms risked renewed pressure on public finances. "We are quite clear that we want the private sector to lead the country," said Aurangzeb. "So our role is to help support, assist any way we can in terms of the ecosystem."

Source: Reuters/ec

MANZANILLO, Mexico: Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 3 storm on Sunday (Oct 11) as it moved parallel to Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that flooded homes. The storm, packing maximum sustained winds of 205kmh, was located about 175km west-northwest of the port city of Manzanillo at 6pm, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said. "Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the forecaster's advisory said. Simon was moving northwest at 7kmh and was expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back toward Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it added.

In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped families remove water from their homes after the storm brought heavy rain overnight. "The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home. "My mother doesn't want to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but she doesn't want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home." Hurricane conditions were likely already occurring within the hurricane warning area and were expected to spread northward overnight, the NHC said. Simon was forecast to bring an additional 50mm to 100mm of rain to parts of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday, with isolated areas receiving up to 200mm more. Total rainfall from the storm could reach 762mm in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas, the NHC said. Dangerous storm surge and destructive waves were also expected along parts of the coast. Mexican authorities placed 28 municipalities across Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under high alert, according to civil protection bulletins. Puerto Vallarta International Airport temporarily closed, while authorities suspended non-essential activities and opened emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities. Earlier on Sunday, President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors as the storm, then a Category 4 hurricane, approached the coast. On Saturday, residents in Manzanillo had appeared largely calm despite the approaching storm, with some businesses boarding up storefronts and civil protection personnel closing beaches and urging people to stay away from the shore. The storm comes days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 hurricane, knocking down trees and power poles and flooding streets.

BANGKOK: Strong investment in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at around 3 per cent, yielding major benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday (Oct 12). The artificial intelligence investment boom was already delivering a "demand shock, an investment shock" that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point,  she said. "AI, love it, hate it. It's already here," Georgieva said. "That shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock," she told hundreds of participants on the first day of a weeklong set of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the Thai capital.

The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday.  Some 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi España, sources familiar with the matter said. AI WILL HAVE PROFOUND CONSEQUENCES Georgieva said AI amounted to a "slow-moving tsunami" that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. "It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live," she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a 30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important producers in the AI supply chain, but many of the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Georgieva said, referencing Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. AI IMPACT ON ENTRY-LEVEL JOBS World Bank President Ajay Banga, who has made jobs a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging "small AI", which is not dependent on large language models, to generate enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. "There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon ... and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," he said. He said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a "new divergence" in growth and job creation between developing and advanced economies. "AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it," he said. "So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI."

Source: Reuters/ec

MELBOURNE, Oct 12 : Four years after New Zealand's heartbreaking Rugby League World Cup semi-final defeat by Australia, halfback Jahrome Hughes is still haunted by a missed opportunity to send the Kiwis into the final. Hughes scored a try and was among New Zealand's best players in the 16-14 loss in 2022, but a speculative grubber kick late in the match squandered a promising attacking opportunity as the Kiwis chased victory. Hughes has carried the regret ever since and is determined to make amends at this year's World Cup, starting with New Zealand's opener against defending champions Australia in Sydney on Thursday. "Getting so close in 2022 in the World Cup and losing to Australia in the semi-final, I still hold a bit of fire in my belly from that," Hughes told reporters on Monday.

"I take a lot of blame for losing that game." Hughes has since established himself among the game's elite playmakers, winning the 2024 Dally M Medal as the National Rugby League's best player with Melbourne Storm and helping New Zealand thrash Australia 30-0 in the 2023 Pacific Championships final on home soil in Hamilton. But the 32-year-old has not played for his country since 2023, with neck and shoulder injuries wiping out his international prospects. He said his return to the national squad had rekindled the excitement he felt as a youngster dreaming of representing the Kiwis. "I've had a couple of years away from them. It just makes you realise you can't take this jersey for granted," he said. "I'm one of the older guys now, but I felt like a little kid coming back into camp yesterday and seeing everyone." New Zealand have not won the World Cup since their breakthrough triumph in 2008, with Australia claiming the last three titles. Hughes hopes a second World Cup title for the Kiwis could boost the game back home, where rugby union and the All Blacks still dominate. "Just thinking back to 2008 when I was a kid and seeing how that win made me feel, if we were able to lift that trophy at the end of this World Cup, the things it would do for the kids back home in New Zealand and all the supporters back home, it would be truly special," he said. In a scheduling quirk, the All Blacks will meet Australia in a rugby union test at Stadium Australia on Saturday, two days after the Kiwis-Kangaroos clash in the same city. Flyhalf Beauden Barrett said he and his All Blacks teammates would cheer on the Kiwis at Sydney Football Stadium before they knuckle down for the second Bledisloe Cup test against the Wallabies. "We've got a bit of free time, so it'll be a great spectacle," Barrett told reporters on Monday. "It's just down the road, too. So, yeah, the town's buzzing."

Source: Reuters
